units.title: Invasive Prenatal Diagnostic Procedures: CVS vs Amniocentesis
units.guide: Invasive prenatal diagnosis provides definitive karyotyping when screening indicates aneuploidy. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) biopsies rapidly dividing cytotrophoblasts at 10-14 weeks, yielding swift results within 48 hours but carrying a 1% procedure-related loss rate and risk of confined placental mosaicism. Amniocentesis samples amniocytes between 15 and 20 weeks with a lower loss rate (<0.5%) and definitive cytogenetic accuracy.

units.title: Amniocentesis Technique, Cordocentesis & Fetal Blood
units.guide: Amniocentesis is performed under continuous real-time ultrasound guidance using a 20-22G spinal needle, aspirating approximately 20 mL of amniotic fluid for cytogenetics, viral PCR, or fetal lung maturity testing. Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS / cordocentesis) accesses the umbilical vein beyond 18 weeks to measure fetal hemoglobin in severe Rh alloimmunization or non-immune hydrops.

units.title: Antepartum Fetal Surveillance Principles & Movement Counts
units.guide: Antepartum fetal surveillance is universally initiated at 32 weeks in high-risk pregnancies (or 2-4 weeks prior to a prior gestational demise). Maternal kick charts, such as the Cardiff 'count-to-10' (10 movements in 2 hours at rest or 12 hours during daily activity), provide a cost-free screening tool; diminished movement reflects early compensatory fetal motor quiescence to preserve central oxygenation.

units.title: Non-Stress Test (NST): Setup, Baseline & Accelerations
units.guide: The Non-Stress Test (NST) evaluates fetal autonomic integrity by recording fetal heart rate (FHR) responses to fetal movement with the mother in a left lateral tilt. A normal baseline FHR spans 110-160 bpm with moderate baseline variability (6-25 bpm). At >=32 weeks, a reactive acceleration requires a heart rate increase of >=15 bpm lasting >=15 seconds (15x15 rule).

units.title: Sinusoidal FHR, Non-Reactive Tracings & Algorithm
units.guide: A sinusoidal heart rate pattern (smooth regular oscillations, 2-5 cycles/min, amplitude 5-15 bpm) is an ominous sign pathognomonic of severe fetal anemia or acute profound acidemia, demanding immediate delivery. Tracings lacking accelerations over 20 minutes are extended to 40 minutes to account for fetal sleep cycle, followed by acoustic stimulation or biophysical scoring if non-reactivity persists.

units.title: Biophysical Profile (BPP / Manning Score) & Modified BPS
units.guide: Manning's Biophysical Profile combines four ultrasound dynamic variables (tone, gross movement, breathing movements, and single deepest pocket >=2 cm) with the NST, scoring each parameter as 0 or 2. Under progressive hypoxic acidemia, early-developing acute neurological centers (NST, breathing) fail first, while the primitive fetal tone center fails last. A score <=4/10 signals significant acidemia and mandates prompt delivery.

units.title: Intrapartum Surveillance Principles & Intermittent Auscultation
units.guide: Uterine contractions physiologically compress intramyometrial blood vessels, transiently reducing intervillous perfusion. While well-oxygenated fetuses tolerate this stress, compromised fetuses develop decelerations and progressive metabolic acidemia. Routine surveillance in low-risk labor utilizes intermittent auscultation (every 30 mins in first stage, every 15 mins in second stage), switching to continuous electronic monitoring for high-risk conditions.

units.title: Cardiotocography: Baseline, Variability & Prolonged Decelerations
units.guide: CTG interpretation assesses baseline rate (110-160 bpm), baseline variability (moderate 6-25 bpm), and decelerations. Absent variability is the most reliable single herald of fetal hypoxia. Prolonged decelerations (drop >=15 bpm lasting 2-10 minutes) commonly arise from uterine tachysystole induced by oxytocin, managed immediately by stopping uterotonics, lateral repositioning, and acute tocolysis.

units.title: Deceleration Morphologies: Early, Late & Variable Decelerations
units.guide: Early decelerations mirror contractions with a nadir coinciding with the peak of the contraction, caused by vagal stimulation from fetal head compression (benign). Late decelerations lag behind contractions with a delayed nadir, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal myocardial hypoxia. Variable decelerations exhibit an abrupt drop caused by umbilical cord compression.

units.title: CTG Categorization (ACOG/FIGO) & Intrauterine Resuscitation
units.guide: Cardiotocography tracings are stratified into Category 1 (Normal/reassuring), Category 2 (Suspicious/indeterminate), and Category 3 (Pathological/non-reassuring). Category 3 tracings (absent variability with late decelerations, severe variable decelerations, bradycardia, or sinusoidal wave) dictate urgent intrauterine resuscitation—discontinuing oxytocin, maternal left lateral positioning, high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus, and rapid delivery.

units.title: Fetal Scalp Blood Sampling, Scalp Stimulation & Pulse Oximetry
units.guide: Fetal scalp blood sampling directly measures capillary pH when CTG is abnormal (>=7.25 normal, 7.20-7.24 pre-acidotic, <7.20 severe acidosis dictating immediate operative delivery). Prior to incision, fetal scalp stimulation that elicits an acceleration confirms a normal pH in virtually 100% of cases, avoiding unnecessary invasive blood sampling.

units.title: Maternal Adaptations: Cutaneous, Uterine & Cervical Shifts
units.guide: Elevated estrogen and progesterone stimulate melanogenesis, producing linea nigra, melasma ('mask of pregnancy'), and palmar erythema. The uterus enlarges dramatically from 50 g to 1100 g, driven predominantly by myometrial hypertrophy. The cervix exhibits vascular engorgement (Chadwick/Goodell signs), glandular hyperplasia forming a protective mucus operculum, and benign columnar ectropion.

units.title: Vaginal Ecosystem, Endocrine Shifts & Fluid Retention
units.guide: Lactobacilli ferment vaginal glycogen into lactic acid, dropping vaginal pH to 3.5-4.0; this acidic shield inhibits bacterial pathogens but predisposes to Candida vulvovaginitis. High placental steroids suppress gonadotropins and maintain decidual quiescence. Maternal fluid retention expands extracellular volume by 6.5-8.5 liters, producing benign dependent edema that readily resolves upon recumbency.

units.title: Maternal Hematological Adaptations & Hemodilution
units.guide: Maternal plasma volume expands by 40-50% while erythrocyte mass increases by only 20-30%, creating physiological hemodilution where hemoglobin normally remains >=11.0 g/dL. Pregnancy induces a marked prothrombotic state: fibrinogen doubles (to 400-600 mg/dL), Factors VII, VIII, IX, and X increase, and fibrinolysis is suppressed, while bleeding and clotting times remain unchanged.

units.title: Maternal Renal, Urinary & Gastrointestinal Adaptations
units.sec: Maternal renal and GI systems · p356-357
units.guide: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, inducing physiological hydroureter (right > left due to dextrorotated uterine compression) and predisposing to ascending pyelonephritis from asymptomatic bacteriuria. Renal blood flow jumps by 70-80% and GFR by 50%, reducing normal serum creatinine to 0.4-0.6 mg/dL. Progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation delays gallbladder emptying and relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, exacerbating GERD.

questions.q: What fetal tissue is aspirated and cultured during Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS)?
opts: Rapidly dividing cytotrophoblast (and mesenchyme) of the chorion frondosum
Desquamated fetal dermal fibroblasts
Amniotic membrane epithelial cells
Fetal nucleated red blood cells
questions.exp: CVS samples mitotic trophoblastic tissue (predominantly cytotrophoblast) of the chorion frondosum. (Book p340)

questions.q: What is the optimal gestational age window for performing Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS)?
opts: 10 to 14 weeks of gestation (ideally 11 to 13 weeks + 6 days)
15 to 20 weeks of gestation
6 to 8 weeks of gestation
18 to 22 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: CVS is performed between 10 and 14 weeks (ideal window 11 to 13w6d); it is contraindicated before 10 weeks. (Book p340)

questions.q: Why is Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) strictly contraindicated before 10 completed weeks of gestation?
opts: It carries a substantial risk of severe fetal transverse limb reduction defects and oromandibular/omphalocele anomalies
It causes immediate maternal Rh sensitization in 100% of cases
It induces premature rupture of membranes in the first trimester
The placenta is not yet attached to the decidua
questions.exp: CVS performed <10 weeks causes fetal vascular disruption, leading to severe limb reduction defects and micrognathia. (Book p340)

questions.q: What is the primary cytogenetic diagnostic disadvantage of Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) compared to amniocentesis?
opts: In 1-2% of cases, results are confounded by Confined Placental Mosaicism (CPM), requiring confirmatory amniocentesis
CVS cannot detect numerical aneuploidies like Trisomy 21
CVS takes 4 weeks to obtain initial karyotype results
Cytotrophoblasts do not possess nuclear chromosomes
questions.exp: Because trophoblast tissue is examined, 1-2% of CVS samples show confined placental mosaicism not present in the fetus, requiring amniocentesis. (Book p340)

questions.q: What is the standard gestational window for performing mid-trimester diagnostic amniocentesis, and what is its associated procedure-related fetal loss rate?
opts: 15 to 20 weeks of gestation (ideal 16-18 weeks); procedure loss rate < 0.5%
10 to 12 weeks of gestation; procedure loss rate 5%
24 to 28 weeks of gestation; procedure loss rate 2%
Any time in the first trimester; procedure loss rate 0%
questions.exp: Amniocentesis is routinely performed between 15 and 20 weeks; the procedure-related loss rate is low (<0.5%). (Book p340)

questions.q: Why is early amniocentesis (performed before 15 weeks of gestation) not clinically recommended?
opts: It is associated with significantly higher fetal loss rates, talipes equinovarus (clubfoot), and fluid leakage
Amniocytes cannot be karyotyped before 15 weeks
The fetal heart is arrested by the needle puncture
Amniotic fluid is devoid of alpha-fetoprotein
questions.exp: Early amniocentesis (<15 weeks) is avoided due to increased risks of miscarriage, amniotic fluid leakage, and orthopedic talipes equinovarus. (Book p340)

questions.q: During diagnostic ultrasound-guided amniocentesis at 16 weeks, what size spinal needle is standardly utilized, and what volume of amniotic fluid is aspirated?
opts: 20 to 22-gauge spinal needle; approximately 20 mL of fluid
16-gauge Trocar needle; 50 mL of fluid
26-gauge butterfly needle; 5 mL of fluid
18-gauge bone marrow needle; 30 mL of fluid
questions.exp: Amniocentesis uses a 20-22G spinal needle under continuous real-time USG guidance, discarding the first 1-2 mL and collecting ~20 mL. (Book p341)

questions.q: In the third trimester, what was the classic indication for performing diagnostic amniocentesis?
opts: Assessing fetal lung maturity via the Lecithin-to-Sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio
Testing for sickle cell anemia carrier status
Measuring fetal head circumference
Assessing maternal alpha-fetoprotein
questions.exp: In the third trimester, amniocentesis was historically performed to assess fetal pulmonary maturity via the L/S ratio (>=2.0 indicates mature lungs). (Book p341)

questions.q: Percutaneous Umbilical Blood Sampling (PUBS / Cordocentesis) is performed under ultrasound guidance starting at >= 18 weeks. Which umbilical vessel is specifically targeted for puncture?
opts: The umbilical vein, near its placental insertion site
The right umbilical artery near the fetal abdominal wall
The ductus arteriosus
The vitelline vein
questions.exp: Cordocentesis samples fetal blood by puncturing the umbilical vein approximately 1 cm from the placental insertion site. (Book p341)

questions.q: What is the primary contemporary clinical indication for performing cordocentesis?
opts: Direct assessment of fetal hemoglobin/hematocrit and direct intrauterine transfusion in severe Rh isoimmunization
Routine first-line screening for Down syndrome
Evaluation of neural tube defect risk
Measurement of maternal serum human placental lactogen
questions.exp: Cordocentesis carries a ~2% procedure-related loss rate and is reserved for diagnostic/therapeutic fetal blood transfusion in severe anemia. (Book p341)

questions.q: What is the most common congenital cardiovascular malformation diagnosed in infants with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)?
opts: Endocardial cushion defect / Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD)
Tetralogy of Fallot
Coarctation of the aorta
Transposition of the great arteries
questions.exp: Endocardial cushion defect (complete AV canal defect) is the most frequent cardiac lesion in Down syndrome, followed by VSD and ASD. (Book p341)

questions.q: In all high-risk pregnancies (e.g., pre-eclampsia, diabetes, IUGR), formal antepartum fetal surveillance is recommended to commence at:
opts: 32 weeks of gestation
24 weeks of gestation
28 weeks of gestation
37 weeks of gestation
questions.exp: Formal antepartum fetal surveillance (NST, BPP) is routinely started at 32 weeks in high-risk pregnancies. (Book p342)

questions.q: When a pregnant woman has a history of an unexplained stillbirth in a previous pregnancy, when should antepartum fetal surveillance begin in the index pregnancy?
opts: 2 to 4 weeks prior to the gestational age at which the previous adverse outcome occurred
At 37 weeks of gestation
From the day of positive pregnancy test
Only when labor contractions begin
questions.exp: Surveillance begins 2 to 4 weeks before the gestational age of the previous stillbirth or adverse fetal outcome. (Book p342)

questions.q: Under the Cardiff 'Count-to-10' protocol for daily fetal movement assessment, fetal activity is considered normal when the mother perceives:
opts: At least 10 discrete fetal movements within 2 hours while resting in the left lateral position (or 10 in 12 hours of normal activity)
At least 3 movements per day
At least 20 movements every hour
At least 1 movement every 10 minutes
questions.exp: Cardiff 'count of 10': perceiving >=10 movements over 2 hours at rest (or within 12 hours during daily activity) is reassuring. (Book p342)

questions.q: What is the primary physiological mechanism leading to decreased fetal movements in chronic placental insufficiency?
opts: Fetal compensatory behavioral adaptation to reduce energy and oxygen consumption in the face of hypoxemia
Complete motor paralysis of the fetal spinal cord
Compression of the fetal brainstem by amniotic bands
Maternal hypoglycemia causing fetal lethargy
questions.exp: Decreased fetal movement is a compensatory survival mechanism to conserve oxygen and nutrients in response to chronic hypoxia. (Book p342)

questions.q: How does an external cardiotocography machine monitor and record fetal well-being during a Non-Stress Test (NST)?
opts: An ultrasound Doppler transducer records FHR and a tocodynamometer records uterine activity, while the mother presses a event marker for fetal movements
A scalp electrode is placed directly on the fetal skull
A pressure catheter is placed inside the amniotic cavity
Maternal pulse oximetry is recorded alongside fetal ECG
questions.exp: External CTG uses two abdominal transducers: an ultrasound transducer for FHR and a tocodynamometer for uterine contractions. (Book p343)

questions.q: What is the normal physiological baseline fetal heart rate (FHR) range on cardiotocography, evaluated over a minimum 10-minute window?
opts: 110 to 160 beats per minute (bpm)
120 to 180 bpm
90 to 130 bpm
100 to 140 bpm
questions.exp: Normal baseline FHR is 110-160 bpm; baseline <110 bpm is bradycardia, and >160 bpm is tachycardia. (Book p344)

questions.q: Normal baseline fetal heart rate variability represents healthy autonomic cardiac control and is quantified as:
opts: Fluctuations of 6 to 25 bpm around the baseline
Fluctuations of < 5 bpm around the baseline
Fluctuations of > 30 bpm around the baseline
Completely flat, unvarying FHR
questions.exp: Moderate (normal) baseline variability is 6-25 bpm, reflecting balanced sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic inputs. (Book p344)

questions.q: At >= 32 weeks of gestation, a reactive fetal heart rate acceleration is strictly defined as an increase in FHR above baseline of at least:
opts: 15 bpm lasting for at least 15 seconds (15x15 rule)
10 bpm lasting for at least 10 seconds (10x10 rule)
20 bpm lasting for at least 2 minutes
30 bpm lasting for at least 30 seconds
questions.exp: At >=32 weeks, acceleration is defined as >=15 bpm above baseline lasting >=15 seconds from onset to return (15x15 rule). (Book p344)

questions.q: If an NST is conducted in a preterm fetus between 28 and 31+6 weeks of gestation, what criteria define an acceleration?
opts: An increase in FHR of >= 10 bpm above baseline lasting for >= 10 seconds (10x10 rule)
An increase in FHR of >= 15 bpm lasting >= 15 seconds
An increase of >= 25 bpm lasting >= 30 seconds
Accelerations are not evaluated before 34 weeks
questions.exp: Before 32 weeks, immature autonomic innervation permits the 10x10 rule (>=10 bpm for >=10 seconds) to qualify as an acceleration. (Book p344)

questions.q: A sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern on cardiotocography is an ominous finding that characteristically indicates:
opts: Severe fetal anemia (e.g., Rh isoimmunization, Parvovirus B19, vasa previa) or acute severe hypoxia/acidemia
Benign physiological fetal quiet sleep
Normal response to maternal food intake
Fetal head compression in the pelvic inlet
questions.exp: A sinusoidal wave pattern (regular sine wave, 2-5 cycles/min, amplitude 5-15 bpm) signifies severe fetal anemia or severe hypoxia/acidosis. (Book p344)

questions.q: What criteria define a 'Reactive' (negative) Non-Stress Test over a 20-minute monitoring period at term?
opts: At least 2 qualifying accelerations (>=15 bpm for >=15s) within 20 minutes with normal baseline and moderate variability
Absence of any fetal heart rate accelerations
Continuous accelerations lasting > 10 minutes
Presence of early decelerations with each contraction
questions.exp: A reactive NST requires >=2 accelerations of >=15 bpm lasting >=15 seconds in a 20-minute window with normal baseline and variability. (Book p345)

questions.q: If an initial 20-minute NST demonstrates fewer than 2 accelerations, what is the mandatory immediate next step?
opts: Extend the monitoring period for an additional 20 minutes (total 40 minutes) to account for the physiological fetal sleep cycle
Perform an immediate emergency Caesarean delivery
Administer high-dose oxytocin infusion
Discharge the patient with reassurance
questions.exp: Normal fetal sleep cycles last 20-40 minutes; an initial non-reactive test must be extended to 40 minutes before declaring it non-reactive. (Book p345)

questions.q: What is the diagnostic accuracy profile of a reactive NST versus a non-reactive NST?
opts: Reactive NST has a very high negative predictive value (>99%); non-reactive NST has a high false-positive rate (~50%) requiring BPS confirmation
Non-reactive NST is 100% specific for fetal death
Reactive NST has a 50% false negative rate
Both tests have identical 90% positive predictive value
questions.exp: A reactive NST reliably predicts normal oxygenation (>99% NPV); however, non-reactive NST has ~50% false positives and must be confirmed by BPS. (Book p345)

questions.q: In Manning's Biophysical Profile (BPP), how are each of the five biophysical parameters scored?
opts: Either 0 (abnormal/absent) or 2 (normal/present), for a maximum composite score of 10
Scored from 0 to 4 based on gestational age
Scored 1, 2, or 3 based on duration
Scored 0 or 1, for a maximum score of 5
questions.exp: BPP evaluates 5 parameters (NST, fetal breathing, gross movement, tone, amniotic fluid), scoring each as either 0 or 2 (maximum 10). (Book p345)

questions.q: To receive a normal score of 2 for 'Amniotic Fluid Volume' in the Biophysical Profile, what ultrasound criterion must be met?
opts: At least one vertical pocket of amniotic fluid measuring >= 2.0 cm in depth (Single Deepest Pocket)
An Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) of >= 15 cm
A fluid pocket completely filled with fetal limbs
A pocket measuring >= 8 cm
questions.exp: A score of 2 for amniotic fluid requires at least one vertical fluid pocket measuring >= 2 cm without umbilical cord or fetal extremities. (Book p345)

questions.q: In progressive fetal hypoxemia and acidemia, in what order are the biophysical parameters compromised and lost?
opts: NST and fetal breathing are lost earliest; gross body movements and fetal tone are lost latest
Fetal tone is lost first, followed by breathing and NST
Amniotic fluid volume is lost immediately within minutes
All parameters cease simultaneously at pH 7.30
questions.exp: Under hypoxia, regulatory centers in the brainstem fail in reverse embryological order: NST and breathing disappear first; tone is lost last. (Book p346)

questions.q: A patient at 38 weeks of gestation undergoes a Biophysical Profile that yields a score of 8/10, but the 2 points lost are for decreased amniotic fluid volume (oligohydramnios). What is the management?
opts: Delivery of the fetus, because oligohydramnios indicates chronic placental insufficiency
Reassurance and repeat BPP in 1 week
Bed rest and maternal IV hydration with discharge
Emergency Caesarean section under general anesthesia within 15 minutes
questions.exp: An 8/10 score with oligohydramnios indicates chronic compromised placental perfusion; delivery is indicated if the pregnancy is >=36-37 weeks. (Book p346)

questions.q: What two components constitute the 'Modified Biophysical Profile' used as an efficient antenatal screening tool?
opts: Non-Stress Test (NST, reflecting acute oxygenation) plus Amniotic Fluid Assessment / SDP (reflecting chronic placental function)
Fetal breathing movements plus umbilical artery Doppler
Fetal tone plus maternal serum AFP
Cardiotocography plus fetal scalp pH
questions.exp: The modified BPP combines the NST (marker of acute fetal acid-base status) with amniotic fluid evaluation (marker of chronic placental perfusion). (Book p346)

questions.q: Why do normal uterine contractions during labor pose a physiological stress to fetal oxygenation?
opts: Myometrial contractions increase intramyocardial/intramural pressure, temporarily compressing spiral vessels and reducing intervillous blood flow
Contractions increase maternal blood pressure to pathological levels
Contractions trigger fetal hypothermia
Contractions cause permanent thrombosis of the umbilical vein
questions.exp: During uterine contractions, intramyometrial pressure exceeds spiral artery pressure, temporarily arresting placental perfusion. (Book p347)

questions.q: According to WHO recommendations for low-risk labor, what is the frequency of intermittent fetal heart sound auscultation during the first and second stages of labor?
opts: Every 30 minutes in the first stage; every 15 minutes in the second stage
Every 15 minutes in the first stage; every 5 minutes in the second stage
Every 60 minutes in the first stage; every 30 minutes in the second stage
Continuous auscultation throughout both stages
questions.exp: In low-risk labor: auscultate every 30 minutes in the first stage (active phase), and every 15 minutes in the second stage. (Book p347)

questions.q: In high-risk intrapartum cases monitored by intermittent auscultation, what is the required frequency of auscultation in the first and second stages of labor?
opts: Every 15 minutes in the first stage; every 5 minutes in the second stage
Every 30 minutes in the first stage; every 15 minutes in the second stage
Every 5 minutes in the first stage; continuously in the second stage
Every 45 minutes in both stages
questions.exp: For high-risk labor: auscultate every 15 minutes during the first stage, and every 5 minutes during the second stage. (Book p347)

questions.q: When performing intermittent auscultation during labor, for how long should the fetal heart rate be counted, and when in relation to a contraction?
opts: Counted for at least 1 full minute, continuing immediately after the end of a uterine contraction
Counted for 15 seconds during the peak of a contraction
Counted for 30 seconds before contractions begin
Counted only during uterine relaxation between contractions
questions.exp: Auscultation is performed for 60 seconds immediately following a contraction to detect potential late decelerations. (Book p348)

questions.q: What is the most common maternal cause of persistent baseline fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm) during active labor?
opts: Maternal fever and intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionitis)
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Epidural analgesia without epinephrine
Maternal hypocalcemia
questions.exp: Maternal pyrexia and chorioamnionitis are the most frequent causes of intrapartum baseline fetal tachycardia. (Book p348)

questions.q: Which parameter on cardiotocography is considered the single most reliable indicator of fetal normoxemia and absence of cerebral acidemia?
opts: Moderate baseline variability (6 to 25 bpm)
Baseline FHR of exactly 140 bpm
Frequent early decelerations
Absence of any uterine contractions
questions.exp: Moderate baseline variability (6-25 bpm) is the single most reliable sign of normal central fetal oxygenation and normal cord pH. (Book p348)

questions.q: A prolonged deceleration on CTG is defined as a decrease in fetal heart rate of >= 15 bpm below baseline lasting for:
opts: At least 2 minutes but less than 10 minutes
At least 30 seconds but less than 1 minute
Greater than 10 minutes continuously
Exactly 15 seconds
questions.exp: A prolonged deceleration is a drop in FHR >=15 bpm lasting >=2 minutes but <10 minutes; if >=10 minutes, it is a baseline change. (Book p349)

questions.q: What is the most frequent iatrogenic cause of acute prolonged fetal heart rate decelerations during induced labor?
opts: Uterine hyperstimulation/tachysystole resulting from oxytocin or misoprostol administration
Administration of prophylactic ampicillin
Artificial rupture of membranes
Maternal oral hydration with water
questions.exp: Excessive uterine activity (hyperstimulation/tachysystole) driven by oxytocin or prostaglandins is the most common cause of prolonged decelerations. (Book p349)

questions.q: Early decelerations on intrapartum CTG are characterized by a gradual decrease in FHR that mirrors the uterine contraction. What is their physiological cause?
opts: Fetal head compression causing transient increased intracranial pressure and vagal stimulation
Umbilical vein compression
Uteroplacental insufficiency
Placental abruption
questions.exp: Early decelerations result from fetal head compression during contractions, eliciting a benign vagal reflex; they are non-hypoxic. (Book p350)

questions.q: Why are late decelerations considered the most ominous deceleration pattern on cardiotocography?
opts: Their nadir occurs after the peak of the contraction, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal myocardial hypoxia
They indicate fetal head compression at the perineum
They reflect rapid cord prolapse through the cervix
They are caused by maternal sleep
questions.exp: Late decelerations lag behind contractions, caused by chemo/baroreceptor triggering from transient hypoxemia in uteroplacental insufficiency. (Book p350)

questions.q: Variable decelerations exhibit an abrupt drop (<30 seconds to nadir) and vary in shape, depth, and duration. What is their primary cause?
opts: Umbilical cord compression
Fetal head compression
Maternal hypothermia
Placental calcification
questions.exp: Variable decelerations are triggered by umbilical cord occlusion/compression (transient umbilical vein and artery collapse). (Book p351)

questions.q: On a cardiotocograph showing variable decelerations, what are 'shoulders' (transient accelerations before and after the deceleration)?
opts: A reassuring compensatory feature indicating healthy fetal autonomic response to transient cord occlusion
An ominous sign of impending cardiac arrest
Artifact produced by maternal coughing
Evidence of fetal seizure activity
questions.exp: 'Shoulders' represent initial venous and late release compensatory accelerations, signaling intact autonomic responsiveness and good prognosis. (Book p351)

questions.q: Under the 3-tier ACOG/FIGO intrapartum CTG classification, what characterizes a Category 1 (Normal / Reassuring) tracing?
opts: Baseline 110-160 bpm, moderate variability (6-25 bpm), no late or variable decelerations, early decelerations present or absent
Absence of any baseline variability with mild tachycardia
Presence of recurrent late decelerations with normal baseline
Sinusoidal pattern with accelerations
questions.exp: Category 1 criteria: baseline 110-160 bpm, moderate variability (6-25 bpm), absence of late/variable decelerations, +/- early decelerations or accelerations. (Book p351)

questions.q: Which of the following CTG abnormalities places a tracing into Category 3 (Abnormal / Non-reassuring)?
opts: Absent baseline variability accompanied by recurrent late decelerations or a sinusoidal pattern
Early decelerations during the second stage of labor
Moderate variability with isolated acceleration
Baseline FHR of 150 bpm without decelerations
questions.exp: Category 3 includes absent baseline variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, bradycardia, or sinusoidal pattern. (Book p351)

questions.q: What is the initial pharmacological step in intrauterine resuscitation when acute fetal decelerations occur in the presence of uterine hyperstimulation?
opts: Immediately discontinue oxytocin infusion and administer terbutaline (0.25 mg SC) for acute tocolysis
Increase oxytocin infusion to accelerate delivery
Administer intravenous methylergometrine bolus
Administer high-dose magnesium sulfate bolus
questions.exp: Immediate intrauterine resuscitation: stop oxytocin, turn to left lateral position, administer IV fluids and O2, and give terbutaline to relax the uterus. (Book p351)

questions.q: What cervical dilatation and fetal station are prerequisite before attempting fetal scalp blood sampling?
opts: Cervix dilated >= 4 to 5 cm with vertex at or below -1.5 station
Cervix dilated 1 cm with floating head
Fully dilated cervix with head on perineum
Cervix closed with intact membranes
questions.exp: Prerequisites for scalp sampling: ruptured membranes, cervix dilated >=4-5 cm, and vertex engaged at least at -1.5 station. (Book p352)

questions.q: What fetal scalp capillary blood pH cutoffs represent normal, pre-acidotic, and acidotic states?
opts: >= 7.25 is normal; 7.20 to 7.24 is pre-acidotic (repeat in 20-30 mins); < 7.20 is acidotic (requires immediate delivery)
>= 7.40 is normal; 7.30 is pre-acidotic; < 7.25 is acidotic
>= 7.10 is normal; < 7.00 is acidotic
>= 7.00 is normal in all labors
questions.exp: Scalp pH: >=7.25 is normal, 7.20-7.24 is borderline/pre-acidotic (repeat in 20-30m), and <7.20 indicates severe acidemia requiring immediate delivery. (Book p352)

questions.q: During digital examination in labor, digital fetal scalp stimulation that elicits a fetal heart rate acceleration (>=15 bpm for >=15s) indicates:
opts: Fetal scalp pH is >= 7.25 in 99-100% of cases, reliably ruling out significant acidemia and avoiding scalp sampling
Severe fetal hypoxia requiring immediate emergency C-section
Cord prolapse into the vagina
Impending uterine rupture
questions.exp: An acceleration in response to scalp stimulation correlates with scalp pH >=7.25 in virtually 100% of cases, reliably excluding acidemia. (Book p352)

questions.q: During intrapartum fetal pulse oximetry, a fetal arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) falling below which threshold is strongly associated with fetal acidosis?
opts: SpO2 < 30% for >= 2 minutes
SpO2 < 90% for 1 minute
SpO2 < 70% for 5 minutes
SpO2 < 50% for 10 minutes
questions.exp: A fetal SpO2 < 30% for at least 2 minutes on continuous intrapartum pulse oximetry correlates with fetal metabolic acidosis. (Book p352)

questions.q: Gestational hyperpigmentation (linea nigra, chloasma/melasma) is primarily driven by elevated estrogen and progesterone stimulating:
opts: Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) and melanocyte sensitivity
Maternal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Prolactin receptor up-regulation
Cortisol degradation in the liver
questions.exp: Estrogen and progesterone stimulate melanocytes and MSH release, producing hyperpigmentation along the midline (linea nigra) and face (chloasma). (Book p353)

questions.q: The non-pregnant uterus weighs approximately 50-60 g and enlarges to approximately 1100 g at term. What is the primary cellular mechanism driving this enlargement?
opts: Myometrial hypertrophy (hyperplasia occurs only in the first trimester)
Myometrial hyperplasia throughout all three trimesters
Deposition of adipose tissue within the perimetrium
Endometrial stromal carcinoma
questions.exp: Uterine enlargement is overwhelmingly due to hypertrophy of existing smooth muscle fibers (hyperplasia is limited to early first trimester). (Book p353)

questions.q: What are Montgomery's tubercles, which become prominent on the maternal breasts by 8-12 weeks of gestation?
opts: Hypertrophied sebaceous glands located on the primary areola
Accessory lactiferous duct orifices
Superficial thrombosed veins of the breast
Ectopic apocrine sweat gland cysts
questions.exp: Montgomery's tubercles are hypertrophic sebaceous glands on the areola that secrete a protective, lubricating lipoid fluid. (Book p354)

questions.q: A pregnant woman presents with painless, minor post-coital vaginal spotting. Speculum examination reveals a red, velvety, glandular outgrowth of endocervical mucosa onto the exocervix. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Cervical ectropion / eversion (benign physiological adaptation; no biopsy required)
Cervical squamous cell carcinoma
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3
Placenta accreta
questions.exp: Eversion of the endocervical columnar epithelium (ectropion) is a physiological response to estrogen; it is benign and requires reassurance. (Book p354)

questions.q: During normal pregnancy, the vaginal pH becomes markedly acidic (pH 3.5 to 4.0) due to:
opts: Döderlein's lactobacilli fermenting estrogen-induced mucosal glycogen into lactic acid
Direct transudation of amniotic fluid into the vaginal vault
Excess secretion of gastric hydrochloric acid
Secretion of acidic mucus from the Bartholin glands
questions.exp: Estrogen increases epithelial glycogen, which Döderlein's bacilli ferment to lactic acid, creating an acidic pH (3.5) protective against pathogens. (Book p354)

questions.q: What is the most common form of infectious vaginitis encountered during pregnancy, thriving in the acidic vaginal microenvironment?
opts: Candida albicans vulvovaginitis
Trichomonas vaginalis
Bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella)
Chlamydia trachomatis
questions.exp: Candida albicans thrives in the acidic, glycogen-rich environment of the pregnant vagina, making candidiasis the most common vaginitis. (Book p354)

questions.q: Why is lactation physiologically suppressed during pregnancy despite maternal prolactin levels rising up to 10-fold by term?
opts: High circulating levels of placental estrogen and progesterone competitively block prolactin action at the breast alveolar receptors
The posterior pituitary fails to synthesize oxytocin
Maternal thyroid hormone inhibits milk synthesis
Prolactin in pregnancy is biologically inactive
questions.exp: Placental estrogen and progesterone block prolactin's secretory effect on alveolar cells; rapid steroid decline after delivery unleashes lactation. (Book p355)

questions.q: How can an examiner clinically differentiate physiological dependent edema of pregnancy from pathological pre-eclamptic edema?
opts: Physiological edema is restricted to dependent lower extremities and subsides with overnight recumbency; pathological edema involves face/hands and persists
Physiological edema is non-pitting, whereas pathological edema is pitting
Physiological edema is accompanied by marked proteinuria
Pathological edema always disappears after walking
questions.exp: Physiological edema occurs in dependent areas (ankles) from IVC compression and resolves with rest; pathological edema is generalized (face, hands) and persists. (Book p355)

questions.q: During normal singleton pregnancy, maternal plasma volume expands by 40-50%, whereas red blood cell volume increases by 20-30%. This physiological mismatch results in:
opts: Physiological hemodilution ('physiological anemia of pregnancy') with decreased hematocrit and blood viscosity
Severe pathological polycythemia
Hemoconcentration predisposing to microvascular ischemia
Decreased cardiac output
questions.exp: Greater expansion of plasma volume over red cell mass causes physiological hemodilution, reducing blood viscosity and cardiac workload. (Book p356)

questions.q: Under standard WHO and CDC definitions, maternal hemoglobin concentration during pregnancy is considered abnormal (anemic) when it falls below:
opts: < 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, or < 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester
< 12.0 g/dL in all trimesters
< 9.0 g/dL in the second trimester
< 13.0 g/dL at any stage
questions.exp: Normal gestational Hb cutoff: <11.0 g/dL in T1 and T3, and <10.5 g/dL in T2 (accounting for maximal mid-trimester hemodilution). (Book p356)

questions.q: What physiological changes occur in maternal leukocyte (WBC) and platelet counts during normal pregnancy and active labor?
opts: Leukocytosis (up to 15,000/mcL in pregnancy, >=25,000/mcL in labor) and mild gestational thrombocytopenia (remains >=100,000/mcL)
Severe leukopenia and thrombocytosis
Pancytopenia across all trimesters
Marked basophilia and severe thrombocytopenia (<50,000/mcL)
questions.exp: Neutrophilic leukocytosis rises up to 15,000 in pregnancy and >=25,000 in labor; benign gestational thrombocytopenia is mild (>=100,000). (Book p356)

questions.q: Pregnancy is a markedly prothrombotic state. Which coagulation factors exhibit significant physiological increases?
opts: Fibrinogen (Factor I increases by 50% to 400-600 mg/dL), Factors VII, VIII, IX, X, and von Willebrand factor
Only Factor XI and Factor XIII
Antithrombin III and Protein S
Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)
questions.exp: Fibrinogen doubles to 400-600 mg/dL, alongside increases in Factors VII, VIII, IX, X, and XII; Protein S and fibrinolysis decline, creating hypercoagulability. (Book p356)

questions.q: Which of the following coagulation parameters remains physiologically UNCHANGED during normal pregnancy?
opts: Bleeding time (BT) and Clotting time (CT)
Fibrinogen levels
Factor VIII activity
Plasma protein concentration
questions.exp: Bleeding time, clotting time, and aPTT remain unchanged in normal pregnancy despite elevation of specific procoagulant factors. (Book p356)

questions.q: Why is physiological hydroureter and hydronephrosis in pregnancy significantly more pronounced on the RIGHT kidney than the left?
opts: Dextrorotation of the enlarging gravid uterus compresses the right ureter against the pelvic brim and crosses the right ovarian vein
The right ureter has thinner smooth muscle walls than the left
The right kidney produces three times more urine than the left
The left ureter is completely immune to progesterone
questions.exp: Uterine dextrorotation places direct pressure on the right ureter at the pelvic brim, combined with right ovarian vein dilatation, making right dilatation marked. (Book p356)

questions.q: In normal pregnancy, maternal Renal Blood Flow (RBF) increases by 70-80% and Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) increases by 50%. How does this alter normal serum creatinine levels?
opts: Serum creatinine falls to a normal range of 0.4 to 0.6 mg/dL; a serum creatinine > 0.8 mg/dL is abnormal in pregnancy
Serum creatinine rises to 1.5-2.0 mg/dL
Serum creatinine remains fixed at 1.0 mg/dL
Serum creatinine is undetectable
questions.exp: Elevated GFR enhances clearance, lowering normal serum creatinine to 0.4-0.6 mg/dL; a level >0.8 mg/dL indicates underlying renal impairment. (Book p357)

questions.q: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy is defined as >= 10^5 CFU/mL of a single pathogen on midstream clean-catch urine. What is the most common causative organism and why is treatment mandatory?
opts: Escherichia coli (80%); mandatory to prevent ascending acute pyelonephritis and preterm labor
Staphylococcus aureus; mandatory to prevent maternal sepsis
Group B Streptococcus; mandatory to prevent maternal liver failure
Proteus mirabilis; mandatory to prevent renal stone formation
questions.exp: E. coli is most common; untreated ASB leads to acute pyelonephritis in 25-30% of pregnant women and increases preterm labor risks. (Book p357)

questions.q: Why is serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) physiologically elevated by two- to three-fold during the third trimester of pregnancy despite completely normal liver function?
opts: Release of large quantities of heat-stable alkaline phosphatase produced by the placental syncytiotrophoblast
Maternal biliary duct obstruction by the gravid uterus
Severe maternal osteomalacia
Fetal bone demineralization
questions.exp: The placenta synthesizes heat-stable ALP (distinguishable from bone/liver heat-labile isoenzymes), doubling or tripling total serum ALP near term. (Book p357)
